title: Relaxation-driven flat bands and topology in moiré transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers
authors: Mitchell Luskin, Max Geier, Liang Fu, Ziyan Zhu
abstract: Moiré transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterobilayers are commonly modeled by a continuum theory that yields topologically trivial bands, in contrast to their homobilayer counterparts which host topological bands and fractional Chern insulators (FCI). We show this conclusion is an artifact of neglecting the pseudomagnetic field generated by lattice relaxation, an effect intrinsic to every moiré material. We develop a continuum model that resolves relaxation into three channels: a modified moiré potential with higher Fourier harmonics, a pseudoelectric (scalar deformation) potential, and a pseudomagnetic (vector) potential. Using WSe$_2$/WS$_2$ as a prototype, we find that the pseudomagnetic field alone gaps the third and fourth valence bands with Chern numbers $\pm 1$ over a broad range of twist angle and lattice mismatch, while the moiré potential correction and pseudoelectric potential narrow the bandwidth and enhance the bandgaps, which survive many-body interactions using neural-network variational Monte Carlo calculations. Relaxation also smoothens the Berry curvature and quantum metric relative to the rigid model, moving the band closer to the ideal Chern limit, beneficial for the quantum anomalous Hall effect, FCI states, and flat-band superconductivity when filled to higher bands. Our work establishes a new framework that connects first-principles calculations, through the continuum model, to many-body observables. Using this framework, we show moiré heterobilayers as a new class of topological materials whose topology is driven entirely by intrinsic lattice relaxation.
summary: The authors introduce an advanced continuum model that accounts for lattice relaxation effects in moiré TMD heterobilayers. They demonstrate that these intrinsic structural deformations are necessary to generate robust topological bands characterized by non-zero Chern numbers. This establishes a powerful new theoretical tool linking fundamental material structure to exotic quantum electronic states.
main_problem: To correct continuum models for moiré TMD heterobilayers by incorporating intrinsic lattice relaxation effects, which are crucial for accurately predicting their electronic topology.
main_result: The pseudomagnetic field alone is sufficient to induce topological gaps with Chern numbers $\pm 1$, and the inclusion of full relaxation enhances these gaps while preserving the topological nature across wide parameter regimes.
method: Developing an extended continuum Hamiltonian that decomposes lattice relaxation into modified moiré potential, a pseudoelectric (scalar) potential, and a pseudomagnetic (vector) potential. Calculations utilize Fourier expansions and neural-network variational Monte Carlo methods.
model_or_system: The system is Moiré transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterobilayers (e.g., WSe2/WS2), modeled by an effective continuum Hamiltonian incorporating strain effects ($\hat{H}_\epsilon$). The analysis compares rigid vs. relaxed electronic structures.
key_observables: Chern numbers ($C_3, C_4$), charge gap ($\Delta_c$), superfluid stiffness ($ ar{D}_s$), Berry curvature, and quantum metric.
important_parameters: Twist angle ($	heta$) and lattice mismatch ($\delta$); the relative strength of interaction energy ($E_C$) to bandwidth ($W_1$).
main_assumptions: The continuum model framework is assumed generalizable; analysis focuses on specific stacking configurations (3R, 2H).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decomposition of relaxation effects on band structure and show phase diagrams mapping topological gaps and Chern numbers across $(	heta, \delta)$ for both 3R and 2H stackings.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the failure of rigid models, then developing the three-channel continuum Hamiltonian, demonstrating that the pseudomagnetic field drives topology, and finally confirming these results using many-body calculations and comparing different stacking symmetries (3R vs. 2H).
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework connecting first-principles DFT calculations to measurable many-body observables like topological gaps and superfluid stiffness in moiré systems, which is highly relevant for understanding emergent quantum phases.
